2611.05674.abstract: While convective motions at the scale of granules on the solar surface are well understood, those of mesogranular and supergranulation are not. At still larger scales, the lack of giant cells is a major mystery. We aim to slightly improve understanding of the radial and horizontal flows associated at mesogranular scales and supergranulation. We perform a deep MURaM small-scale dynamo simulation, extending from $50$~Mm below the solar surface and with a horizontal size of 60~Mm and sufficient resolution to begin to properly resolve the magnetic bright points in intergranular lanes. We determine the structure of the convective modes from the simulations at different scales, and compare the power spectra to those which have been previously observed. At all scales which are resolved by the simulation the simulated flows agree with the amplitude implied by Doppler measurements and local correlation tracking (LCT) measurements. The power in the vertical Doppler velocities at supergranular and larger scales is shown to be influenced by density perturbations near the surface. The structure of the modes at depth is simple as expected from the previous study of \cite{LordCameron2014} except the horizontal forcing scale scales like $H_\rho^{2/3}$ instead of $H\rho$. The simulations reproduce the observations up to scales of $60$~Mm. Within the simulated range, $l>=70$, we do not see the excess power associated with the convective conundrum.

2611.05760.title: How fast is the fastest-rotating O-type star in the Galaxy?

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison between the observed spectrum of LAMOST J040643.69+542347.8 (black) and the best-fitting ZPEKTR model (red). Top panel: Full displayed spectral range 4050–4600 Å. The shaded grey area indicates the range spanned by the first quartile of the $\chi^{2}_{\rm rel}$ distribution, and the dotted teal lines mark the main spectral features. 2611.05760.abstract: {Rapid rotation distorts massive stars, making parameters from spherical models inclination-dependent. We studied these effects in the extreme Galactic O-type runaway LAMOST J040643.69+542347.8.} {We re-determined its stellar and rotational parameters with an oblate, gravity-darkened photospheric model and tabulated Stark profiles for selected \ion{He}{ii} lines.} {We fitted continuum-normalised spectra over 4000--4600\,Å with \texttt{ZPEKTR}, using TLUSTY/SYNSPEC emergent fluxes, limb darkening to weight their angular contribution over the visible Roche surface, Espinosa-Lara \& Rieutord gravity darkening, and Schöning--Butler Stark profiles. Interstellar and wind- or circumstellar-dominated features were masked.} {The model reproduces \ion{He}{ii}~$\lambda4200$, \ion{He}{i}~$\lambda4471$, and \ion{He}{ii}~$\lambda4542$. We obtained parent non-rotating counterpart (PNRC) parameters $T_{\rm eff}^{\rm PNRC}=38\,716\pm1041$~K, $\log g^{\rm PNRC}=4.12\pm0.12$, and $v_{\rm e}\sin i=587\pm73$~\kps. The central grid solution gives $\Omega/\Omega_{\rm c}=0.93$, $v_{\rm e}/v_{\rm c}=0.77$, $i=65^\circ$, $R_{\rm e}/R_{\rm p}=1.25$, and an equatorial centrifugal-to-gravitational acceleration ratio $\eta_{\rm e}=0.50$. Roche critical rotation requires $\eta_{\rm e}=1$ and $R_{\rm e}/R_{\rm p}=1.5$: despite the high angular rate, the central solution is not critical in equatorial force balance. The projected velocity exceeds, but is statistically consistent with, the previous spherical-fit value.} {\object{LAMOST J040643.69+542347.8} has a markedly oblate, gravity-darkened photosphere. Its proximity to critical rotation should be assessed using $\Omega/\Omega_{\rm c}$, $v_{\rm e}/v_{\rm c}$, and $\eta_{\rm e}$ together. A controlled spherical fit with the same atmosphere grid is needed to isolate the bias from neglecting deformation and gravity darkening.}

2611.05833.abstract: We present the discovery and photometric study of a distant dwarf nova KSP-OT-201803a using BVI-band observation data obtained by using the KMTNet Supernova Program. One superoutburst (SO) and three normal outbursts are identified from two years of observations (2018-2019), which show that KSP-OT-201803a is an SU UMa-type dwarf nova (DN). Applying the phase dispersion minimization method to the superhump data during the plateau phase of the SO yields a superhump period of P_sh = 127.4 minutes (=2.123 hr =0.08847 days). By stacking ten images of the quiescent phase, we find the quiescent phase magnitude of V = 22.59 +/- 0.18 mag. The SO shows quiescent-to-peak amplitude of 4.97 +/- 0.18 mag and duration of 16.59 days which are typical for the SU UMa-type DNe. Using the superhump period-orbital period relation of SU UMa stars, we obtain the approximate distance of 3.7 +/- 0.3 kpc to KSP-OT-201803a and Galactocentric distance of 9.4 kpc and height from the Galactic plane of +1.2 kpc. Stars at these large distances may belong to the Galactic halo or thick disk, which contain old, metal-poor Population II stars; therefore, these systems may have undergone a different evolutionary process than Population I objects. The orbital period gap of DNe spans 2.45-3.18 hours. Assuming that the orbital period of KSP-OT-201803a is a few percent shorter than its superhump period, KSP-OT-201803a may have just emerged from the period gap and recently resumed mass transfer after crossing its lower boundary.

2611.05881.abstract: A comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic analysis of TIC 349005337, a highly active M-type detached eclipsing binary with an orbital period of 2.6079133 days, is presented utilizing high-cadence and long-term monitoring photometry from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and medium-resolution spectroscopy from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST). By integrating radial velocity curves with light curves, we determined the fundamental physical parameters for both components. The system consists of an M-dwarf primary ($M_1 = 0.517 \pm 0.009 M_\odot$, $R_1 = 0.518 \pm 0.003 R_\odot$) and a fully convective secondary ($M_2 = 0.298 \pm 0.004 M_\odot$, $R_2 = 0.357 \pm 0.003 R_\odot$). A total of 12 high-energy stellar flares, with the most energetic event reaching $3.87 \times 10^{34}$ erg, is identified, confirming the system is in a state of magnetic hyper-activity. The frequent superflares suggest that intense magnetic activity and significant starspot coverage play a dominant role in altering the stellar atmospheric structure. As the secondary component falls below the fully convective boundary, these energetic flares provide critical empirical constraints for distributed dynamo models in the low-mass regime. Our results highlight TIC 349005337 as an ideal laboratory for investigating the interplay between binary dynamics, magnetic reconnection, and the resulting impact on the atmospheric stability of potential orbiting exoplanets.

2611.05902.abstract: Polar crown filaments (PCFs) are crucially related to the structure of solar polar magnetic fields. They are physically significant because of the ``rush-to-the-pole'' motion, which is an indicator of the poleward drift of magnetic fields from decayed active regions. The formation and evolution of PCFs offer important insights into the Sun's magnetic activity at high latitudes and the solar cycle variation. In this study, we present a collective analysis of 50 PCF disappearance events covering solar cycle 24 and 25. Among them, 24 show rotational motions, and nine have sufficiently clear magnetic configurations for comparison with numerical model predictions. In all nine events, the observed rotation directions agree with the model predictions, suggesting possible magnetic-flux-rope-like structures in these events. All except one of the PCFs in our sample disappeared through eruption rather than thermal disappearance, and most associated CMEs were slow ($<800$ km s$^{-1}$). For events accompanied by transient coronal holes, the estimated magnetic flux associated with the dimming regions is on the order of $10^{20}$--$10^{21}$ Mx. Time--distance analysis identifies 22 events with a clear slow-rise to fast-rise transition, with onset heights ranging from several tens to about 160 Mm and a mean onset velocity of about 2.8 km s$^{-1}$ after excluding the highest-velocity event. Together, these findings characterize the magnetic structure and dynamics of PCF eruptions.

2611.05934.abstract: We investigate two successive tiny quiet-Sun EUV ejections on 2022 October 29 using coordinated Solar Orbiter/EUI, IRIS, SDO/AIA, and Goode Solar Telescope observations. We examine their low-lying geometry and the chromospheric and transition-region response before and between the releases. A curved H-alpha thread is present beforehand, and Mg ii and Si iv spectra reveal a compact multithermal precursor 2.6--2.7 min before the first EUV brightening. EUI--AIA stereoscopy places the recurrent compact EUV kernel near 2.2 Mm and the sampled emission at approximately 0.6--4.2 Mm along inclined, locally arched structures. The first ejection shows multithreaded, helical-looking EUV strands; the second shows straighter strands and a decrease in the cross-ridge separation of redshifted and blueshifted Mg ii k3 samples from 1.47'' to 0.89''. Nevertheless, the two peaks have comparable emission-measure increments and estimated event-associated thermal contents of a few 10^26 erg under the same assumptions. Before the second ejection, the regional Si iv and k3 blueshift signals remain enhanced, while the Mg ii central reversal along the activated ridge remains shallower than before the event. Component reconnection between the curved structure and the surrounding field offers a possible explanation. The observations show that jet-like EUV emission can occur in low-lying structures. The second ejection begins before the chromospheric and transition-region spectra have returned to their pre-event states. Its spectral signatures may therefore depend on the atmospheric changes associated with the first ejection as well as on the additional energy input.

2611.05995.abstract: We utilize spectroscopic and imaging data from the EIS/Hinode and the AIA/SDO to determine plasma and wave parameters along coronal fan loops. We determined the temperature along the loop lengths using the EM-loci method with EIS spectral lines and identified multi-thermal plasma components at temperatures ranging from 0.8-1.05, 1.2-1.4, and 1.6-1.8 MK. We further compared these temperature distributions along the loops with those derived from DEM analysis carried out using AIA coronal passbands. The multi-thermal nature of coronal fan loops can be well resolved using EIS spectroscopic data. We determined the density along the loop using the line-ratio method from the EIS Fe XII line pair. We found that density decreases slowly from the expected hydrostatic equilibrium. Our results demonstrate the multi-thermal nature of overdense loops, which can be well resolved with EIS spectroscopic data. We also determined the velocity amplitude of Alfvén waves from the non-thermal broadening of EIS Fe XII spectral line profiles. We further estimated the Alfvén wave energy flux in the corona by combining these parameters with the recently reported magnetic field strength of $\approx$200 G at the coronal footpoint of fan loops. The estimated Alfvén wave energy flux is $\approx$ 2$\times 10^7$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, significantly higher than those reported in earlier studies, and can contribute to coronal losses due to radiation along the fan loops in the active region.

2611.06548.abstract: We present a new circular polarisation survey of approximately 100 white dwarfs selected as featureless DC stars and combine our measurements with previous observations. Our compilation contains 205 objects, of which 24 show firm circular polarisation detections, while another four show marginal signals that require confirmation. Four magnetic white dwarfs originally classified as DC show polarisation spectra with significant contributions from spectral lines. Depending on the treatment of these objects and of the marginal detections, the inferred fraction of magnetic objects in the DC selected sample lies between approximately 10 and 14%. Among objects without identifiable line contributions, the circular polarisation never exceeds approximately 2%, substantially below the levels observed in some hotter magnetic white dwarfs with prominent spectral features. This is unlikely a symptom of field decay, since in our sample we find no significant evidence for a dependence of magnetic incidence on cooling age, and magnetic fields are detected in stars with cooling ages exceeding 9 Gyr. Instead, strong spectral line opacity provides a natural mechanism for producing much larger polarisation amplitudes than the continuum. In the full sample considered here, the incidence of detectable magnetism increases with stellar mass. Most average-mass magnetic stars for which repeated observations are available show no clear polarimetric variability, whereas variability appears more common among the most massive objects.

2611.06549.abstract: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.

2611.06650.abstract: Massive stars strongly influence their environments through their radiation, stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, while their own evolution is strongly shaped by wind mass loss. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterised by strong, optically thick winds, and the implementation of these winds remains an important uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region. We investigate the effects of incorporating these latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) metallicities. We find that the temperature dependence of the WR wind can significantly alter the evolution of stars near the threshold for WR formation. In particular, an implementation that transitions from a hydrogen rich WNL wind prescription to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at temperatures of approximately 70 to 90 kK. This produces a concentration of models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars, a feature that has previously been difficult to explain with stellar evolution models. Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically motivated, temperature dependent WR winds can improve the agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations.

2611.05470.abstract: The intermediate neutron-capture process ($i$-process) has been invoked to explain the peculiar compositions of carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars enriched in both slow- ($s$) and rapid- ($r$) neutron-capture elements. Recent literature has questioned its operation at higher metallicities, but observational evidence remains limited. We analyse Gemini/GHOST and McDonald/Tull spectra of six $\rm -0.7 < [Fe/H] < -0.1$ stars identified in GALAH by their extreme Ba and Eu (or Sm) compositions ($\gtrsim$10$\times$ solar). We also reanalyse archival spectra of two literature $i$-process candidates. We determine abundances in up to 42 elements (Li through Pb), $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, and Mg isotopic ratios, and compare to literature barium and CEMP stars and multiple asymptotic giant branch (AGB) model grids. Three stars exhibit extreme [Pb/Fe] (+1.79$\pm$0.19 to +2.50$\pm$0.32 dex), and two extreme [Eu/Fe] (+1.10$\pm$0.11 to +1.30$\pm$0.11 dex), distinguishing them from typical metal-rich barium stars. Two of these three exhibit abundance patterns that are inconsistent with $s$-process models and best explained by existing $i$-process predictions. The remaining sample is either consistent with $s$-process enrichment or suggestive of atomic diffusion. Both literature candidates are well-fit by the $i$-process model, but conventional $s$-process enrichment cannot be excluded. Our findings reinforce that metal-rich AGB stars contribute to the production of elements classically attributed to the $r$-process. These results identify promising candidates for $i$-process enrichment near solar metallicity and motivate additional $i$-process models to understand the contribution of this nucleosynthetic process to the chemical evolution of the Milky Way disk.

2611.05536.abstract: Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) provides astrometric measurements for more than a billion sources, hundreds of thousands of which have non-single-star astrometric solutions that indicate deviations from linear proper motion. Although sources with orbital solutions have been extensively inspected for compact objects via the astrometric mass function, two other solution types--the 7-parameter constant-acceleration solutions characterized by $\dot{\mathbf{\mu}}$, and the 9-parameter variable-acceleration solutions characterized by $\dot{\mathbf{\mu}}$ and $\ddot{\mathbf{\mu}}$--have not been as carefully explored. In this work, we develop a methodology for selecting sources within the Gaia DR3 9-parameter non-single-star astrometric solutions that are most likely to host massive compact companions. We assume that a source is the luminous star in a binary orbit around a dark object and derive analytic expressions for the sky-projected accelerations and jerks for three binary populations with different orbit approximations: inclined eccentric, face-on eccentric, and face-on circular. Using POSYDON, we develop a fourth, more realistic population of binaries, each consisting of a luminous star and a black hole. For each population, we address observational biases using gaiamock and select only the systems it fits with a 9-parameter solution. We find that binaries likely to host massive compact companions can be identified from the characteristic joint astrometric accelerations and jerks exhibited by the luminous stars, despite 9-parameter fits under-constraining full orbits. Finally, to illustrate the utility of our approach, we analyze a historical object of interest, HD 12871, and examine 9-parameter fits of Gaia BH3-like binaries.

2611.05694.abstract: Persistent radio sources (PRSs) associated with repeating fast radio bursts probe the immediate magneto-ionic environment of their engine and thereby constrain the nature and evolutionary stage of the progenitor. The persistent radio source of FRB20201124A is the most extreme in the current sample, with a spectrum that remains flat or inverted up to 22 GHz. We aim to constrain the centimetre-to-millimetre spectral energy distribution of this source and to test whether its properties are consistent with a young, rotation-powered magnetar wind nebula. We analysed archival ALMA Band 3 observations at $\sim100$ GHz and combined them with existing VLA measurements at 6, 15 and 22 GHz. The resulting spectrum was fitted with the Granot--Sari broken power law in the slow-cooling regime using Bayesian nested sampling. The two-parameter model yields a peak frequency $u_m = 63^{+100}_{-33}$ GHz and a peak flux $F_m = 28\pm9$ $\mu$Jy. This solution is consistent with theoretical expectations for a young magnetar wind nebula, which predict a peak frequency in the same range and a self-absorption frequency below $\sim0.5$ GHz. With its inverted spectrum extending to tens of gigahertz and the highest peak frequency among known PRSs, the source associated with FRB20201124A is the most extreme in the current sample. Its properties match those expected for a rotation-powered magnetar wind nebula, making it a strong candidate for the youngest ($t\lesssim20$ yr) magnetar associated with a repeating FRB to date.

2611.05740.abstract: M dwarf stars represent prime targets for the detection and characterization of small, temperate exoplanets; however, their complex activity and convective surfaces pose significant challenges for high-resolution spectroscopic studies. This work aims to investigate the impact of stellar convection on high-resolution spectroscopic observations of M dwarf stars and develop an integrated approach combining 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations, spectroscopic modeling, and transit analysis to mitigate stellar noise. We employ 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations of M dwarf stellar convection to generate synthetic spectra. We compare the synthetic spectra to actual observations of GJ 3470. We model a high-resolution transit sequence of the Neptune-size GJ 3470 b, including centre-to-limb variations (CLVs) and the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect (RME), and process the sequence via principal component analysis (PCA) to de-trend stellar effects. Comparison of synthetic spectra with actual observations shows that current H2O line lists remain inaccurate, with modest agreement in line strength and position for the chosen K-band interval. During the transit of GJ 3470 b, the amplitude of CLVs+RME is comparable to exoplanet signals. Current PCA can in principle de-trend such effects, but its behaviour is highly dependent on the copresence of telluric and planetary signals. While we are able to correctly detect the exoplanet with no evident bias from stellar residuals, this result is limited to a narrow spectral interval and a specific orbital configuration. This study demonstrates that 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations are essential for accurately modeling convection-induced spectral variability in M dwarfs. Our integrated framework establishes a foundation to obtain unbiased measurements from future ELT observations of exoplanets orbiting M dwarfs.

2611.05880.abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers excite a Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (KHI) in the shear layer between them. It is parasitized upon by the magnetic field to form a powerful magnetic dynamo. Using a large ensemble of high-resolution visco-resistive KHI-driven dynamo simulations we construct analytical, asymptotic in Reynolds number ($\rm{Re}$) models for the magnetic field growth rates and mean vertical field dynamo onset times. Our models suggest that in the $\rm{Re} \gg 1$ limit, the mean vertical field is seeded immediately, kinematic growth rates become asymptotic in $\rm{Re}$, and the dynamo moves out of the kinematic stage on $\mathcal{O}(0.1\,\rm{ms})$ timescales, readily attaining magnetar-strength fields during this transition. This suggests that most global BNS merger simulations are not time-resolving the correct KHI-driven dynamo regime.

2611.06249.abstract: We present the optical $BVR$ polarization measurements for the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17 from its giant outburst in early 2023 and subsequently over three years. We detect a significant polarization of about $\approx1.1$--$2.1\%$, which includes the interstellar contribution. Polarization evolves significantly with time since the outburst. The interstellar polarization was found to be $\approx2.5$--$2.9\%$. The obtained intrinsic optical polarization of LS V +44 17 after correction is between $0.5$--$1.7\%$, perpendicular to the interstellar polarization direction. We consider various plausible sources of optical polarization and infer scattering in the Be decretion disk to be the most dominant source based on time and spectral evolution. Changing intrinsic PA with time hints at a plausible precession of the Be disk.

2611.06640.abstract: Sparse observations of binary pulsars can leave the orbit and the pulse count across observing gaps uncertain. We present APOLLO-Timing, a Bayesian phase-orbit lattice method that fits timing parameters together with integer pulse offsets between observing sessions. PINT checks the candidate connections at fixed pulse numbers. For PSR J1912-1215, a preliminary Keplerian fit to variations in the apparent spin period and its derivative did not phase-connect 96 times of arrival (TOAs) spanning 1438.07 days in 23 sessions. Starting from its position, spin frequency F0, and first time derivative F1 estimated in that fit, with dispersion measure fixed, APOLLO-Timing recovers the orbit and a unique best-supported phase-connected solution without supplied orbital parameters. A repeat full-data blind search recovers the same pulse counts in 914.0 s, including the final fit. Setting the initial F1 to zero in the 17, 18, and 19 session subsets also recovers the reference path. The solution gives Pb = 17.526 days, x = 23.448 light-seconds, e = 2.65e-5, chi-square = 188.01, and a weighted rms residual of 5.08 microseconds. For a pulsar mass of 1.4 solar masses and inclination of 60 degrees, the inferred companion mass is 0.67 solar masses, favoring a CO/ONeMg white dwarf.

2611.06723.abstract: Observations of the Crab pulsar (PSR B0531+21) during solar conjunction probe plasma structure in the inner solar wind through radio-propagation effects. We analyze dispersion measure (DM) and rotation measure (RM) measurements from the annual conjunctions of 2022-2026, obtained with the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME). The 2025 DM time series is distinguished from those of the other years by a secondary enhancement on 21 June, about one week after the main conjunction peak. In our scattering-corrected DM measurements, this feature, $\Delta$DM $= (3.95 \pm 0.20) \times 10^{-3}$ pc cm$^{-3}$, is about 20 times the day-to-day DM scatter outside the conjunction window. The RM time series, measured by combining the single pulses of each observation and corrected for the ionospheric contribution, show conjunction excursions of up to $\sim 60$ rad m$^{-2}$ and changes of sign consistent with crossings of heliospheric magnetic-sector boundaries, but no counterpart to the secondary 2025 DM feature or to a similar post-conjunction DM tail in 2026. From the slope of the RM excess against the DM excess we estimate the electron-density-weighted line-of-sight magnetic field; for the sectors with significant slopes, $|\langle B_\parallel \rangle|$ is at least $\sim 0.2$ to $\sim 10$ mG near conjunction, largest in 2025.

2611.06735.abstract: The mechanism for accelerating energetic particles in the outer heliosphere is still under debate. The termination shock, turbulence, and magnetic reconnection have all been proposed as viable mechanisms. We investigate compression-driven particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection in the heliospheric current sheet using the MHD--SDE framework that incorporates energetic-particle feedback into the MHD evolution. For the heliosheath conditions considered here, we find that reconnection-driven acceleration is inefficient downstream of the termination shock, whereas reconnection near the heliopause can generate stronger compression and produce a power-law differential intensity spectrum $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-5.4}$. However, even the hardest spectrum achieved during magnetic reconnection remains much steeper than the typical $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-1.5}$ spectrum observed in the heliosheath. This indicates that magnetic reconnection alone is insufficient to explain the acceleration of energetic particles in the heliosheath.

2611.06763.abstract:
Solar flares are among the most dramatic events in the solar system, releasing substantial magnetic energy and accelerating a large number of electrons to high energies. Notably, in certain events, the above-the-looptop region may contain a significant population of nonthermal electrons, both in number and energy. For the first time, we adopt a novel numerical method that combines magnetohydrodynamics with energetic particles incorporating feedback from nonthermal electrons to investigate electron acceleration and transport in solar flares. We find that a large fraction of energetic electrons are accelerated via the current sheet and termination shock regions. Most energetic electrons are concentrated in the above-the-looptop region, carrying a sizable amount of the released energy.
We observe that greater feedback of nonthermal electrons leads to steeper energy spectra. The energy density of the nonthermal electrons oscillates due to the periodic impact of magnetic islands into the above-the-looptop, which may help explain the observed quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs). Our simulations provide new insights into the origin of nonthermal electrons and associated emissions in the above-the-looptop region.
